title: Robotics & Physical Systems
desc: ROS, kinematics, state estimation, motion planning, and SLAM — enriched with NU ME495 Northwestern University content.

watch.title: Hello (Real) World with ROS — TU Delft (edX, free on OCW)
watch.focus: Week 1: ROS Essentials — nodes, topics, services, actions. Watch the ROS Essentials video (1.1.1). Focus on: what a node is, what a topic is, how they communicate via publish/subscribe. This is the architecture of every ROS system you will build.

concept.title: Robots are systems, not just models
concept.body:
A robot system has four layers: Sensing (cameras, LiDAR, IMU), Perception (your CV/ML work), Planning (deciding what to do), Actuation (motors, arms). ROS (Robot Operating System): middleware that connects all layers.

In ROS, nodes are processes, topics are communication channels. Each node publishes/subscribes to topics. This decoupling lets you swap out perception modules without changing the control code — critical for research.
concept.analogy: A robot is like a company with departments. ROS is the company Slack — every department publishes updates, subscribes to relevant channels, and acts on incoming information without knowing who sent it.
concept.visual:
ROS architecture:
Node A (camera) → publishes /image_raw
Node B (detector) → subscribes /image_raw, publishes /detections
Node C (planner) → subscribes /detections, publishes /cmd_vel
Node D (motors) → subscribes /cmd_vel

Key tools:
rostopic list  → see all active topics
rostopic echo /detections  → debug live data
rqt_graph  → visualize node connections

challenge.q: Your perception node publishes detections at 30Hz, but your planning node processes at 10Hz. What ROS feature prevents the planner from being overwhelmed?

opts.t: ROS automatically throttles publishers to match subscriber rate
Message queues: the subscriber has a queue_size parameter that buffers or drops messages
ROS topics are synchronous — publisher waits for subscriber
The faster publisher is automatically slowed down

challenge.hint: What mechanism in publish/subscribe architectures handles rate mismatches between producers and consumers?
challenge.exp: Message queues with configurable queue_size. The planning node processes the most recent message in its queue — older messages are dropped if the queue is full. This is by design: the planner should use the most recent perception data, not stale data from 3 seconds ago.

units.title: Coordinate Frames & Transforms
units.meta: SE(2), SE(3), TF, rigid body motion — NU ME495

watch.title: NU ME495 Lecture 2 — 2D Transforms Review
watch.focus: Read sections: Overview, 2D Rigid Body Transforms, Transformation Matrix. Focus on: why we need frames, what the transformation matrix encodes, and the "thought experiment" in the notes — it builds the right intuition.

concept.title: Every measurement needs a reference frame — and transforms connect them
concept.body:
In robotics, every sensor measurement is in a different coordinate frame. A camera sees an object at (x,y,z) in the camera frame. The robot needs it in the world frame to act on it.

A 2D rigid body transform T ∈ SE(2) combines rotation AND translation in one matrix. A 2D pose (x, y, θ) becomes a 3×3 homogeneous transformation matrix. Chaining transforms: T_world_object = T_world_robot · T_robot_camera · T_camera_object.

ROS tf manages this chain automatically — it tracks all transform relationships over time and lets you query "where is the object in the world frame?" at any timestamp.
concept.analogy: You see a coffee cup 30cm to your right (in YOUR frame). To tell a robot arm where it is, you need to express it in the arm's base frame. tf does this automatically — you describe each frame relationship once, and it computes all the rest.
concept.visual:
2D Transform T ∈ SE(2):
T = [[cos θ, -sin θ, x],
     [sin θ,  cos θ, y],
     [0,      0,     1]]

Transform a point p=[px, py, 1]:
T·p = [(cos θ)px - (sin θ)py + x,
       (sin θ)px + (cos θ)py + y, 1]

Chain: T_AC = T_AB · T_BC

challenge.q: You have T_world_robot (robot pose in world) and T_robot_camera (camera pose on robot). How do you get the position of a detected object (given in camera frame) in world frame?

opts.t: p_world = T_world_robot + T_robot_camera + p_camera
p_world = T_world_robot · T_robot_camera · p_camera (matrix multiplication chain)
p_world = T_robot_camera · T_world_robot · p_camera
You need a separate calibration step — transforms cannot be chained

challenge.hint: Transform chains: to go from camera frame to world frame, you compose the transforms in order: camera → robot → world.
challenge.exp: p_world = T_world_robot · T_robot_camera · p_camera. Matrix multiplication composes the transformations in sequence. Order matters — T_AB · T_BC takes you from C to A, NOT B to A. This is the most common robotics coordinate transform mistake. The NU ME495 "thought experiment" in the notes is worth reading to build the intuition for why the order works this way.

units.title: URDF & Sensor Integration
units.meta: Robot description, joint types, multi-sensor fusion

watch.title: Building a Visual Robot Model with URDF — ROS Official Tutorial
watch.focus: Read: "Building a Visual Robot Model with URDF from Scratch". Focus on: links, joints, the tree structure of a URDF, and how joint types (revolute, prismatic, fixed) correspond to physical robot constraints.

concept.title: Describing your robot so ROS understands it
concept.body:
URDF (Universal Robot Description Format): XML describing robot geometry, joints, and physical properties. Links = rigid bodies. Joints = connections (revolute, prismatic, fixed). Every tf frame in your robot corresponds to a link in the URDF.

Sensor integration: different sensors run at different rates and in different frames. time synchronization (message_filters.ApproximateTimeSynchronizer) aligns data from sensors running at different rates. Calibration gives you the transform between sensor frames.
concept.analogy: URDF is like an assembly manual for the robot — it tells ROS exactly how every part connects to every other part. Without it, ROS cannot compute the tf chain that maps between sensor frames.
concept.visual:
URDF structure:
<link name='base_link'><visual>...</visual></link>
<joint name='joint1' type='revolute'>
  <parent link='base_link'/>
  <child link='arm_link'/>
  <axis xyz='0 0 1'/>
  <limit lower='-1.57' upper='1.57'/>
</joint>

Time sync:
camera 30Hz + LiDAR 10Hz
→ ApproximateTimeSynchronizer(slop=0.05s)
→ synchronized pairs

challenge.q: Your robot has camera (30Hz) and HC-SR04 (10Hz). You want to fuse them. What is the fused output rate, and what is the core challenge?

opts.t: 30Hz — use camera rate, interpolate HC-SR04
10Hz — limited by the slower sensor; challenge is that data is from different times and frames
20Hz — average of both rates
1Hz — sensors must be fully synchronized before fusion

challenge.hint: The fused output requires data from both sensors. What limits the fused output rate?
challenge.exp: 10Hz — the slower sensor limits fusion rate. The core challenge is dual: (1) temporal — camera and HC-SR04 data are from slightly different times; and (2) spatial — they measure from different physical positions (different frames). Time synchronization handles (1), calibration handles (2). Both must be solved for reliable sensor fusion.

chapters.title: Kinematics & Dynamics
chapters.sub: 2D transforms · DH · IK · Odometry — NU ME495

units.title: Differential Drive Kinematics
units.meta: Derive kinematics, twist, center of rotation — NU ME495

watch.title: NU ME495 Lecture 3 — Derive Kinematics + Lecture 4 — Odometry
watch.focus: How wheel velocities produce a body twist (v, ω). The concept of the Instantaneous Center of Rotation (ICR). Why the odometry equations come from the kinematic constraints. Read both Derive Kinematics and Odometry lectures.

concept.title: How wheel velocities become robot motion
concept.body:
For a differential drive robot, left wheel velocity v_l and right wheel velocity v_r produce a body twist: linear velocity v = (v_r + v_l)/2 and angular velocity ω = (v_r - v_l)/d where d is the track width.

The robot moves along an arc whose center of curvature (ICR) is at distance R = v/ω from the robot center. When v_l = v_r: straight line (ICR at infinity). When v_l = -v_r: pure rotation (ICR at center).

Integrating the twist gives the new pose. This is odometry — accumulating pose from wheel encoder readings.
concept.analogy: Differential drive is like a boat with two paddles. Both paddles forward: straight ahead. Right paddle faster: turn left. Left paddle backward: spin in place. The twist tells you the instantaneous motion; integrating it tells you where you ended up.
concept.visual:
v_l = ω_l · r,   v_r = ω_r · r   (r = wheel radius)
Linear vel:  v = (v_r + v_l) / 2
Angular vel: ω = (v_r - v_l) / d   (d = track width)
Radius of curvature: R = v / ω

ICR cases:
v_l = v_r  → ω=0, straight line (ICR at ∞)
v_l = -v_r → v=0, pure spin (ICR at center)

challenge.q: A differential drive robot has wheel radius r=0.1m, track width d=0.3m. Left wheel: ω_l=2 rad/s, Right wheel: ω_r=3 rad/s. What is the radius of curvature R?

opts.t: R = 0.5m (turning left)
R = 1.5m (turning left)
R = 1.5m (turning right)
R = 0.3m (tight turn)

challenge.exp: v_l=0.2, v_r=0.3. v=(0.3+0.2)/2=0.25 m/s. ω=(0.3-0.2)/0.3=0.333 rad/s. R=0.25/0.333=0.75m. The right wheel is faster, so the robot turns LEFT, moving along a leftward arc with radius 0.75m. Use the interactive widget above to verify — set wl=2, wr=3 and step forward.

watch.title: Robotic Manipulation — MIT (manipulation.csail.mit.edu)
watch.focus: Chapter on kinematic description of robot arms, forward kinematics, and how coordinate frames chain together. Read the online notes — they include interactive simulations.

concept.title: From joint angles to end-effector position
concept.body:
Forward kinematics: given joint angles θ, compute end-effector pose. Each joint is described by 4 DH parameters (a, α, d, θ). The transform for joint i is a 4×4 homogeneous matrix. FK = product of all joint transforms.

Inverse kinematics: given desired end-effector pose, find joint angles. Harder than FK — multiple solutions or no solutions. Jacobian IK: ẋ = J(θ)·θ̇, so θ̇ = J⁺·ẋ. Iterate until position error ≈ 0. Use damped least squares J⁺=(JᵀJ+λI)⁻¹Jᵀ near singularities.
concept.analogy: FK is like knowing how to fold a map — given the fold angles, you compute where the tip lands. IK is the reverse: given where you want the tip, find the fold angles. Often multiple solutions exist (your arm can reach a point in many configurations).
concept.visual:
DH Transform per joint i:
T_i = Rot_z(θ_i)·Trans_z(d_i)·Trans_x(a_i)·Rot_x(α_i)
FK: T_0_n = T_0_1 · T_1_2 · ... · T_{n-1}_n

Jacobian IK:
ẋ = J(θ)·θ̇
θ̇ = J⁺·(x_target - x_current)
Iterate: θ_{k+1} = θ_k + α·θ̇_k
Damped: J⁺ = Jᵀ(JJᵀ+λI)⁻¹  ← handles singularities

challenge.q: Your Jacobian IK solver fails when the robot arm is fully extended straight. What is happening and the fix?

opts.t: Target position is unreachable — arm needs to be shorter
Kinematic singularity: Jacobian is rank-deficient at full extension, pseudo-inverse becomes unstable → use damped least squares
Jacobian IK only works for 3-DOF arms
The algorithm has a numerical bug

challenge.hint: What happens to the Jacobian matrix when all joints are aligned and the robot has no "elbow room" to maneuver?
challenge.exp: Kinematic singularity: at full extension, certain joint motions produce no end-effector motion. J loses rank → J⁺ becomes numerically unstable (entries → ∞). Damped least squares: J⁺=(JᵀJ+λI)⁻¹Jᵀ adds λI to avoid division by near-zero. λ is small normally (no damping) but prevents instability near singularities. This is the standard industrial solution.

units.title: Dynamics & Physical Constraints
units.meta: Equations of motion, torques, gravity compensation

watch.title: UCLouvain — Modeling and Simulation of Multibody Systems Part I (edX, audit free)
watch.focus: Week 2-3: dynamics of multibody systems — equations of motion, torques, forces. Focus on: Newton-Euler formulation for robot arms, how torque requirements are computed, and the ROBOTRAN tool that generates Python code from your dynamic model.

concept.title: Forces, torques, and physical reality
concept.body:
Kinematics tells you where. Dynamics tells you how hard. Robot dynamics: τ = M(θ)θ̈ + C(θ,θ̇)θ̇ + G(θ). M=inertia matrix, C=Coriolis/centripetal, G=gravity.

Gravity compensation: command τ = G(θ) to counteract gravity — the arm stays in place despite gravity. This is the simplest practical use of dynamics and it is used in every real robot arm.

Why this matters for ML: a neural network that ignores torque limits will produce physically impossible commands that real hardware will refuse or that will damage actuators.
concept.analogy: Kinematics: where can the robot reach (geometry). Dynamics: what force does it need to get there and stay there (physics). A surgeon needs both: where to cut (kinematics) and how hard to press (dynamics).
concept.visual:
Robot dynamics:
τ = M(θ)·θ̈ + C(θ,θ̇)·θ̇ + G(θ)

τ: joint torques (what motors provide)
M: inertia (resistance to acceleration)
C: Coriolis (velocity-dependent forces)
G: gravity (holding configuration upright)

Gravity compensation: τ_cmd = G(θ)
→ net torque = 0 → arm stays in place

challenge.q: Robot arm holds a 2kg surgical instrument horizontally 0.4m from the elbow. Motor max torque = 10Nm. Can the motor hold this?

opts.t: No — 2kg is too heavy for any motor at 0.4m
No — gravity torque = 7.84Nm which exceeds the 10Nm limit
Yes — gravity torque = 2×9.8×0.4 = 7.84Nm < 10Nm limit. Motor can hold it with 21% margin.
Cannot determine without joint angle information

challenge.hint: Gravity torque = mass × g × lever arm distance = 2 × 9.8 × 0.4. Compare to motor limit.
challenge.exp: Gravity torque = 2 × 9.8 × 0.4 = 7.84Nm. 7.84Nm < 10Nm → motor can hold it with 2.16Nm margin. This is the calculation you do before any robot deployment in medical or industrial settings. Always verify torque margins before commanding a new configuration.

chapters.title: Probability, Gaussians & State Estimation
chapters.sub: Probability review · Gaussian RVs · EKF · NU ME495

units.title: Probability for Robotics
units.meta: Bayes theorem, Gaussian RVs, noise models — NU ME495

watch.title: NU ME495 Lecture 7 — Probability Review + Lecture 9 — Gaussian Random Variables
watch.focus: Read both lectures. Focus on: Bayes theorem applied to sensor fusion, the jointly Gaussian distribution (mean vector μ, covariance matrix Σ), and the key result: linear transformation of a Gaussian is still Gaussian. This is what makes the Kalman filter tractable.

concept.title: Probability is the language of robot uncertainty
concept.body:
Robots are uncertain. Sensors are noisy. Actuators are imperfect. Probability is how we represent and reason about that uncertainty.

From NU ME495: a jointly Gaussian random variable X ~ N(μ, Σ) has mean vector μ and covariance matrix Σ. Its level sets are ellipsoids. Key result: if X ~ N(μ,Σ) and Y = AX + b, then Y ~ N(Aμ+b, AΣAᵀ). This linearity is why Kalman filters work — linear transforms of Gaussians stay Gaussian.

The conditional distribution is the key to Bayesian estimation: given some measurements, what is our updated belief about the robot state?
concept.analogy: Probability in robotics is like a doctor's reasoning: 'The patient has symptom A (sensor reading). Given my prior knowledge and this symptom, what is the probability of disease B (robot state)?' Bayes theorem formalizes this update.
concept.visual:
Gaussian: X ~ N(μ, Σ)
μ ∈ R^k: mean vector
Σ ∈ R^{k×k}: covariance (positive definite)

Level sets: (x-μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x-μ) = c (ellipsoids)
Large σ² → wide ellipse → high uncertainty
Small σ² → narrow ellipse → low uncertainty

Linear transform: Y=AX+b → Y~N(Aμ+b, AΣAᵀ)
This is WHY Kalman filter works.

challenge.q: A robot pose estimate is X ~ N([2,3]ᵀ, [[0.1,0],[0,0.5]]). What does the covariance matrix tell you about the uncertainty?

opts.t: Equal uncertainty in all directions — covariance is always symmetric
Higher uncertainty in the y-direction (σ²_y=0.5 > σ²_x=0.1) — the ellipse is taller than it is wide
The robot is more likely to be at (3,2) than (2,3)
The off-diagonal zeros mean x and y positions are perfectly correlated

challenge.hint: Diagonal elements of Σ are variances per dimension. Off-diagonal elements are covariances between dimensions. What do the magnitudes tell you?
challenge.exp: σ²_x=0.1, σ²_y=0.5. The uncertainty in y is 5× larger than in x. The confidence ellipse is elongated in the y-direction — the robot knows its x-position much better than its y-position (e.g., it has been moving along a wall in the x-direction). Off-diagonal zeros mean x and y uncertainty are independent (uncorrelated). This kind of structured uncertainty appears constantly in SLAM.

units.title: Kalman Filter from Scratch
units.meta: Predict, update, Kalman gain — NU ME495

watch.title: NU ME495 Lecture 10 — Kalman Filter
watch.focus: Read the full lecture. Focus on: the predict step (uncertainty grows), the update step (uncertainty shrinks via Kalman gain), and the derivation of the Kalman gain K = P⁻H/(HPH+R). Understand why K balances between the prediction and the measurement.

concept.title: The optimal filter for linear Gaussian systems
concept.body:
The Kalman filter maintains a Gaussian belief about the state: mean x̂ and covariance P. Two steps per timestep:

Predict: x̂⁻ = Ax̂ + Bu (state propagates via dynamics). P⁻ = APAᵀ + Q (uncertainty grows with process noise Q). Update: K = P⁻Hᵀ(HP⁻Hᵀ + R)⁻¹ (Kalman gain). x̂ = x̂⁻ + K(z - Hx̂⁻) (measurement pulls the estimate). P = (I-KH)P⁻ (uncertainty shrinks).

The Kalman gain K balances: when R is large (noisy sensor), K is small (trust the prediction more). When Q is large (unpredictable dynamics), K is large (trust the measurement more).
concept.analogy: The Kalman filter is the mathematical version of a detective reasoning under uncertainty. 'My prediction says the suspect is here (prior). The witness says they saw them there (measurement). I'll combine both, weighting by how reliable each source is (Kalman gain).'
concept.visual:
Kalman Filter cycle:

PREDICT:
  x̂⁻ = A·x̂ + B·u      (predict state)
  P⁻ = A·P·Aᵀ + Q      (uncertainty grows)

UPDATE:
  K = P⁻·Hᵀ·(H·P⁻·Hᵀ + R)⁻¹  (Kalman gain)
  x̂ = x̂⁻ + K·(z - H·x̂⁻)     (correct estimate)
  P = (I - K·H)·P⁻              (uncertainty shrinks)

Q: process noise (dynamics uncertainty)
R: measurement noise (sensor uncertainty)

challenge.q: In the Kalman update step, if R → 0 (perfect sensor), what does K become and what does this mean?

opts.t: K → 0 — perfect sensor means we ignore it
K → H⁻¹ — we fully trust the measurement, prediction is ignored
K → I — standard identity update
K → ∞ — the filter becomes unstable

challenge.hint: K = P⁻Hᵀ(HP⁻Hᵀ + R)⁻¹. What happens as R → 0?
challenge.exp: As R→0: K → P⁻Hᵀ(HP⁻Hᵀ)⁻¹ = H⁻¹ (for square H). This means x̂ = x̂⁻ + K(z-Hx̂⁻) = x̂⁻ + H⁻¹(z-Hx̂⁻) = H⁻¹z — we completely trust the measurement and discard the prediction. When the sensor is perfect, why would you trust the noisy dynamics? Conversely, as R→∞ (terrible sensor), K→0 and we fully trust the prediction. Use the interactive widget above — drag R to 0.1 and watch how the posterior snaps to the measurement.

units.title: Extended Kalman Filter
units.meta: EKF linearization, robotics SLAM preview — NU ME495

watch.title: NU ME495 SLAM Implementation Notes (PDF) — EKF section
watch.focus: Focus on pages covering EKF: the linearization step (Jacobian instead of exact transform), why we need EKF for nonlinear systems like robot pose estimation, and the structure of the EKF predict/update cycle.

concept.title: Kalman filter for nonlinear systems
concept.body:
The standard Kalman filter assumes linear dynamics (Ax) and linear measurements (Hx). Robot systems are nonlinear: the odometry equations (sin, cos) are nonlinear, and landmark measurements (atan2) are nonlinear.

EKF solution: linearize at the current estimate using the Jacobian. Replace A with F = ∂f/∂x|_{x̂} and H with G = ∂h/∂x|_{x̂}. Then run the standard KF equations with these local approximations. Works well when nonlinearities are mild and the estimate is close to the truth.
concept.analogy: The EKF is like replacing a curved road with its tangent line at your current position. The tangent line (Jacobian) is a good local approximation — and you recompute it at every step as you move, so you're always working with a fresh local approximation.
concept.visual:
EKF vs KF:
KF:  predict: x̂⁻ = A·x̂
     update:  K = P⁻·Hᵀ·...

EKF: predict: x̂⁻ = f(x̂)     ← nonlinear f
             F = ∂f/∂x |_{x̂} ← Jacobian of f
             P⁻ = F·P·Fᵀ + Q
     update:  G = ∂h/∂x |_{x̂} ← Jacobian of h
             K = P⁻·Gᵀ·(G·P⁻·Gᵀ+R)⁻¹
             x̂ = x̂⁻ + K·(z - h(x̂⁻))

challenge.q: You have a robot at pose [x,y,θ] and observe a landmark at range r and bearing φ. The measurement model h(x,y,θ) = [sqrt((lx-x)²+(ly-y)²), atan2(ly-y, lx-x) - θ] is nonlinear. Why does EKF work here but standard KF cannot?

opts.t: Standard KF can handle this — atan2 is just a special case of a linear function
Standard KF requires H to be a matrix (linear measurement model). atan2 is nonlinear — EKF linearizes h at the current estimate via Jacobian G = ∂h/∂x
EKF is always better than KF regardless of linearity
The issue is that the state is 3D — KF only works in 1D

challenge.hint: KF assumes z = Hx (linear). What category does atan2(ly-y, lx-x) - θ fall into?
challenge.exp: atan2 is nonlinear — it cannot be expressed as Hx for any matrix H. Standard KF would require linearizing it manually and using a fixed approximation (which would be wrong everywhere except the linearization point). EKF computes the Jacobian G = ∂h/∂x at the current state estimate — a local linear approximation that is updated every timestep. This is valid as long as the estimate error is small relative to the nonlinearity scale, which it typically is in well-designed SLAM systems.

units.title: Path Planning — RRT & Configuration Space
units.meta: C-space, RRT, A* — visual and interactive

watch.title: MIT Robotic Manipulation — Motion Planning (manipulation.csail.mit.edu)
watch.focus: Chapter: Geometric Pose Estimation and planning sections. Focus on: configuration space concept, why obstacles in Cartesian space become forbidden regions in C-space, and sampling-based planning (RRT). The textbook includes interactive Drake simulations you can run in the browser.

concept.title: From goal to collision-free trajectory
concept.body:
Configuration space (C-space): the space of all possible robot configurations (joint angles). A robot pose is a point in C-space. Obstacles in Cartesian space map to regions in C-space. Planning in C-space reduces the problem to finding a path between two points while avoiding forbidden regions.

RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree): grows a tree by sampling random configurations, extending toward them, and checking for collisions. Fast for high-dimensional spaces. A*: optimal on a grid but exponential in dimension — impractical for 6-DOF arms.
concept.analogy: C-space: instead of thinking 'avoid that wall', think 'avoid these joint angle combinations that would put my arm through the wall'. Planning in C-space turns the physical obstacle avoidance problem into finding a path on a map — much cleaner.
concept.visual:
RRT algorithm:
1. Sample random q_rand in C-space
2. Find nearest node q_near in tree
3. Extend tree from q_near toward q_rand by step δ
4. Check collision: does the new config hit an obstacle?
5. Add to tree if collision-free
6. Repeat until goal is reached

A* complexity: k^n cells for n-DOF robot
k=100, n=6: 10^12 cells → infeasible
RRT: ~1000-10000 samples → tractable

challenge.q: Your 6-DOF robot arm uses grid-based A* in joint space with 100 values per joint. How many C-space cells does this create, and why is RRT preferred?

opts.t: 600 cells — 100×6. Manageable.
10^12 cells — curse of dimensionality. RRT samples randomly and is tractable in any dimension.
10^6 cells — the number scales linearly with joints, not exponentially.
A* is always preferred — it finds the optimal path.

challenge.hint: A* discretizes the space into a grid. How many cells does a 6D grid with k values per dimension have?
challenge.exp: k^n = 100^6 = 10^12 cells — completely infeasible. This is the curse of dimensionality: grid-based methods scale exponentially with the number of dimensions. RRT samples randomly without discretizing — it works in any dimension by exploring the space tree-like, focusing samples where the tree has not yet reached. Use the interactive widget above to see how the tree explores space and finds a path.

watch.title: Brian Douglas PID Control tutorial series
watch.focus: What each PID term does (P=proportional response, I=integral accumulated error, D=derivative anticipation), why all three are needed together, and how to tune them systematically.

concept.title: The most used controller in the world
concept.body:
PID: u(t) = Kp·e(t) + Ki·∫e(τ)dτ + Kd·de/dt. P: responds to current error — immediate response but may overshoot. I: accumulates error over time — eliminates steady-state error. D: rate of change — anticipates and dampens oscillations.

For robotics: each joint has a PID controller tracking desired position/velocity. Your planning layer sends desired positions; the PID layer commands motor torques. Anti-windup: clamp the integral term to prevent it from accumulating during saturation.
concept.analogy: P: how hard you push based on how far you are from target (more error = more force). I: builds up if you are consistently off — like accumulated debt you must pay. D: brakes as you approach to prevent overshoot — feeling the rate of change and slowing down proactively.
concept.visual:
u(t) = Kp·e + Ki·∫e dt + Kd·ė
e(t) = desired - actual

High Kp: fast response but oscillates
High Ki: eliminates steady error but can wind up
High Kd: dampens oscillations but amplifies noise
Anti-windup: integral_term = clip(integral, -max, max)

challenge.q: Your robot joint PID controller has a persistent 2° steady-state error (always 2° below target even when stable). Which term to increase and why?

opts.t: Kp — more proportional gain will push harder toward target
Ki — integral term accumulates the persistent error over time and generates corrective action proportional to the total accumulated error
Kd — derivative term will help reach the target faster
All three need retuning simultaneously

challenge.hint: Steady-state error (constant offset that persists after transient dies) is exactly what the integral term is designed to eliminate. What does the integral of a constant error equal?
challenge.exp: Ki. Steady-state means ė=0 (no change) and the P term = Kp·e balances some opposing force (friction, gravity, etc.). Adding more Kp would just reach a different steady-state. The I term accumulates: ∫e dt = e·t → grows over time → eventually large enough to overcome the friction/gravity. Once error=0, integration stops and the integral term holds the corrective action. This is the fundamental purpose of the I term.

watch.title: Stanford AA289 Robotics Seminars — YouTube Playlist

concept.title: Beyond PID: learning and optimization
concept.body:
MPC (Model Predictive Control): at each timestep, solve an optimization problem over a receding horizon H. Minimize cost (energy, time, tracking error) subject to dynamics constraints and input limits. Apply first control, re-plan. More systematic than PID tuning, handles constraints explicitly.

Imitation learning: learn a control policy by watching expert demonstrations. Behavior cloning = supervised learning on (state, action) pairs from an expert. Sim-to-real gap: policies trained in simulation fail on real hardware due to dynamics mismatch, sensor noise, actuator delays.
concept.analogy: PID: reactive — respond to current error. MPC: plan ahead — solve 'what should I do in the next 10 steps to reach my goal best?' while respecting all constraints. Imitation learning: learn by watching an expert, not by trial and error.
concept.visual:
MPC:
At time t, solve:
min Σ_{k=0}^{H} cost(x_k, u_k)  [horizon H=10]
s.t. x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k)  (dynamics)
     u_k ∈ [-u_max, u_max]  (input limits)
     x_k ∈ X_feasible        (state constraints)
Apply u_0, re-plan at t+1

Sim-to-real gap mitigations:
→ Domain randomization (vary sim params)
→ System identification (fit real dynamics)
→ Adaptive control (update online)

challenge.q: You train a robot grasping policy in simulation with perfect perception. On real hardware with slightly displaced objects it fails. Beyond standard distribution shift, what specific sim assumption is violated?

opts.t: The policy architecture is too simple — use a larger network
Sim-to-real gap: simulation has perfect state estimation, zero actuator delays, exact dynamics — all violated on real hardware simultaneously
The policy needs more imitation learning data
Grasping requires a different control algorithm

challenge.hint: What does simulation assume that real hardware violates? Think about: state estimation, timing, physics.
challenge.exp: Sim-to-real gap is multi-dimensional: (1) perfect state estimation in sim vs perceptual uncertainty on hardware, (2) zero actuator delay in sim vs 10-50ms hardware delays, (3) exact dynamics in sim vs joint friction, cable stretch, motor saturation on hardware. Domain randomization (randomly varying sim parameters during training) is the standard mitigation — it exposes the policy to a wide range of conditions, making it robust to the real-world variation.

units.title: SLAM — Simultaneous Localization and Mapping
units.meta: EKF-SLAM, state augmentation, landmark initialization — NU ME495

watch.title: NU ME495 SLAM Implementation Notes (full PDF)
watch.focus: Read all sections. Focus on: how the robot pose and landmark positions are combined into one big state vector, how new landmarks are added (state augmentation), and how the EKF predict/update cycle works when both robot pose and landmark positions are uncertain.

concept.title: Building a map while figuring out where you are
concept.body:
SLAM: simultaneously estimate robot pose AND build a map of the environment. The challenge: you need the map to localize, and you need localization to build the map. EKF-SLAM solves both together by maintaining a joint Gaussian over [robot pose, all landmark positions].

State vector: [x, y, θ, lx₁, ly₁, lx₂, ly₂, ...] — robot pose plus all landmark positions. Each new landmark augments the state (adds 2 dimensions). The covariance matrix captures correlations between robot pose and landmark positions — this is what makes EKF-SLAM powerful.
concept.analogy: SLAM is like being blindfolded in an unknown room. You can feel the walls (sensor measurements) and count your steps (odometry). SLAM combines both — your step count updates your position estimate, and each wall contact updates both your position AND your map of where the walls are. The map and your position get better together.
concept.visual:
EKF-SLAM state vector:
ξ = [x, y, θ, lx₁, ly₁, ..., lxN, lyN]
Dimension: 3 + 2N (grows with each new landmark)

Covariance Σ:
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  Σ_rr  │  Σ_rl₁  │  Σ_rl₂  │  robot-landmark correlations
│  Σ_l₁r │  Σ_l₁l₁ │  Σ_l₁l₂ │
│  Σ_l₂r │  Σ_l₂l₁ │  Σ_l₂l₂ │
└─────────────────────────────┘
When robot moves → all correlations update
When landmark observed → robot position tightened

challenge.q: In EKF-SLAM, the robot moves and the covariance of ALL landmarks increases, even those far from the robot. Why?

opts.t: This is a bug — only nearby landmarks should be affected by robot motion
Landmarks are defined relative to world frame, and the robot pose uncertainty propagates to all landmark estimates through the cross-covariance terms Σ_rl
The EKF predict step always increases all uncertainties by the same amount
Only landmarks within sensor range are affected by robot motion

challenge.hint: Look at the EKF-SLAM covariance structure. What do the Σ_rl terms (robot-landmark cross-covariance) represent?
challenge.exp: The cross-covariance terms Σ_rl capture the correlation between robot pose uncertainty and landmark position uncertainty. When the robot moves (odometry update), robot pose uncertainty grows. Because the landmarks were originally localized relative to the robot, this uncertainty propagates through Σ_rl to all landmarks. This is correct behavior — if you are less certain where the robot is, you are less certain where everything is. The magic of SLAM is that seeing a known landmark in the update step DECREASES robot pose uncertainty AND all landmark uncertainties simultaneously.

units.title: Circle Detection from Sensor Data
units.meta: Arc fitting, HC-SR04 scan, NU ME495 algorithm

watch.title: NU ME495 Lecture 13 — Circle Fitting (Al-Sharadqah and Chernov algorithm)
watch.focus: Read the full algorithm (14 steps). Focus on: why this is a machine learning problem (fitting a model to data), the SVD step, and the RMSE computation. This algorithm is specifically designed for partial arcs — exactly what your HC-SR04 radar scan produces.

concept.title: Detecting circular objects from arc measurements
concept.body:
Your HC-SR04 radar scan (from Hardware Section Project 5) produces a set of (angle, distance) points. If a cylindrical obstacle is in range, these points form an arc. The NU ME495 algorithm (Al-Sharadqah and Chernov) fits a circle to partial arc data — specifically designed for laser/ultrasonic scan data.

Why it is an ML problem: you have data (points) and you are learning a model (circle center + radius) to explain that data. The SVD step finds the best-fit circle by minimizing algebraic distance — a form of least squares.
concept.analogy: Circle detection is like looking at footprints in a circle and inferring where the center of the circle was — even if you only have footprints from one quarter of the circle. The algorithm reconstructs the full circle from partial arc data.
concept.visual:
NU ME495 Circle Fit Algorithm (14 steps):
1. Compute centroid (x̄, ȳ)
2. Shift to centroid: xᵢ = x̂ᵢ - x̄
3. Compute zᵢ = xᵢ² + yᵢ²
4. Form data matrix Z (n×4)
5. Moment matrix M = Z^T Z / n
6. Constraint matrix H
7. Compute H⁻¹
8. SVD of Z = UΣVᵀ
9. If σ₄ < 10⁻¹²: A = 4th column of V
10. Else: solve eigenvalue problem
11. Extract center (a,b) and radius R
12. Shift back: center = (a+x̄, b+ȳ)
13. Compute RMSE
Output: (center_x, center_y, radius, RMSE)

challenge.q: Your HC-SR04 radar scan gives 8 points that form a partial arc (~60° of a circle). The circle fit gives RMSE=0.3cm. A new scan gives 12 points over ~20° arc. RMSE=2.1cm. Why is the wider arc better despite fewer points needing a fit?

opts.t: More points always give better fits — 8 points is insufficient
Arc length determines geometric constraint: a 60° arc strongly constrains center+radius, but a 20° arc looks nearly like a line — the circle fit is underconstrained
The second scan must have had more noise
RMSE and arc length are unrelated

challenge.hint: Think about fitting a circle to a tiny arc vs fitting it to a larger arc. What does a very small arc look like geometrically?
challenge.exp: Geometric constraint. A 20° arc is nearly indistinguishable from a straight line — infinitely many circles (of different radii) can fit through it equally well. The fit is underconstrained, leading to high RMSE and unreliable radius/center estimates. A 60° arc has clear curvature — the circle center and radius are well-determined. In practice: reject circle fits where the arc spans less than a minimum angle (typically 20–30°) and RMSE exceeds a threshold.

units.title: Data Association
units.meta: Mahalanobis distance, landmark matching — NU ME495

watch.title: NU ME495 Lecture 14 — Data Association for SLAM
watch.focus: Read the full lecture. Focus on: why nearest-Euclidean distance fails (ignores covariance), what Mahalanobis distance adds (accounts for uncertainty shape), and the provisional landmark concept (avoid adding spurious landmarks).

concept.title: Matching new measurements to known landmarks
concept.body:
In SLAM, when you take a new measurement, you must decide: is this a known landmark, or a new one? Wrong associations corrupt the entire SLAM estimate — a single wrong association can cause the filter to diverge.

Mahalanobis distance: d = (z - ẑ)ᵀ Ψ⁻¹ (z - ẑ), where Ψ = G·P·Gᵀ + R is the predicted measurement covariance. This distance is normalized by uncertainty — "how many standard deviations away is this measurement from what I expected?" Smaller Mahalanobis distance = better match.

From NU ME495: temporarily add a new landmark for each measurement. If all existing landmarks have Mahalanobis distance above a threshold, the measurement is from a new landmark.
concept.analogy: Mahalanobis distance is like asking 'is this person my friend Bob, given that Bob is usually somewhere in this area (with uncertainty)?' Euclidean distance says: 'how far are they from Bob's last known position?' Mahalanobis says: 'how far are they from Bob's last known position, scaled by how uncertain I am about Bob's position?' If I'm very uncertain, someone quite far away might still be Bob.
concept.visual:
Data association algorithm (NU ME495):
1. N = number of known landmarks
2. For measurement zᵢ:
   a. Temporarily add landmark N+1 at h⁻¹(zᵢ)
   b. For each landmark k (including N+1):
      - Compute Ψ_k = G_k·P·G_kᵀ + R
      - Compute d_k = (zᵢ-ẑ_k)ᵀ·Ψ_k⁻¹·(zᵢ-ẑ_k)
   c. Set d_{N+1} = threshold (e.g., 10.0)
   d. Match to landmark with minimum d_k
   e. If match is N+1: add new landmark

challenge.q: Two landmarks L1 at x=1.0 (σ=0.1) and L2 at x=1.0 (σ=2.0) are at the same position but with different uncertainties. A measurement arrives at x=1.5. Euclidean says both are equidistant. What does Mahalanobis say?

opts.t: Mahalanobis also says both are equidistant — same result as Euclidean here
Mahalanobis says L1 is FARTHER away (5σ) and L2 is CLOSER (0.25σ) — the measurement is more consistent with uncertain L2
Mahalanobis says L1 is closer because it has smaller uncertainty
Mahalanobis cannot be computed when two landmarks are at the same position

challenge.hint: Mahalanobis distance = (x-μ)²/σ². Compute for each landmark. Which landmark is this measurement more surprising for?
challenge.exp: d_L1 = (1.5-1.0)²/0.01 = 25 (5 standard deviations — very surprising!). d_L2 = (1.5-1.0)²/4.0 = 0.0625 (0.25 standard deviations — not surprising at all). Measurement associates with L2. This makes sense: L2 is very uncertain (σ=2), so being 0.5m off is expected. L1 is precise (σ=0.1), so being 0.5m off is almost impossible (5σ). Use the interactive widget to verify — set landmark positions equal and vary uncertainty.
